I had originally started this response with a very snarky comment. Re-reading your post, I don't feel that you intended to offend; but others might not be so analytical.

Looking back on it, I wish I had added "the original text" to the title. I believe that the Constitution is a living document and its meaning does change over time. I think it's the first half of the amendment "A well regulated militia being necessary to the security of a free state" is the part that has become obsolete. And several referenced court rulings by other people in this thread support that claim.

edit: And I just realized how unoriginal my post is now that i think about it. It's essentially boiled down to: "A 200+ year old document can't be taken literally because of changing context." Not just the 2nd Amendment.

The meaning does not change over time. The meaning is static. Despite any technological advances, or anything else, the intentions remain the same - certain inalienable rights cannot be denied. Even if the context changes, we have rights that cannot legally be denied, ignored, or subverted. Illegally is another matter.

The "meaning" behind the 2nd amendment was partly protection against outside forces (lack of standing army) AND protection from itself. The argument pointed out above is that you can't protect yourself from drones and bombs with a pistol/rifle, which is true, (and also incorrect/straw-man, but that's another issue) but the meaning of protecting the people from the government is definitely still there and valid! A good example of this interpretation of meaning as static is encryption.

The US Govt. at one time classified any strong encryption as a "weapon". Argue that the people need to fight against the government to keep them from trampling all over our other rights, and use the government's argument of "encryption is a weapon", and bam: the 2nd amendment in a modern context.

"The right of the people to be encrypted shall not be infringed" is far to specific and not something the framers could have imagined though, but the static meaning of the 2nd amendment lets us keep the ideals alive.

edit: I realized I sounded like I was arguing that the 2nd amendment protects encryption. I'm not a constitutional lawyer and don't wish to make that argument, but simply to say that we should look at what the intent of the framers was, in the context of their time, and understand what our actual values and ideals are. An expansive and inclusive view of what we ought to be in America, rather than a reductionist "they clearly didn't mean semi-automatic weapns, only muskets allowed" viewpoint.
